title: Classes and Objects
description: Understand the foundation of OOP: how to define classes with fields, properties, methods, and constructors, and how to instantiate objects from those blueprints.

data.text: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is built on the idea of modeling real-world things as **classes** and **objects**. A class is a blueprint that defines what data an object holds and what actions it can perform. An object is a concrete instance created from that blueprint. In C#, almost everything you work with — from simple strings to complex UI controls — is an object created from a class.

A class is a user-defined type that bundles **data** (fields/properties) and **behavior** (methods) into a single unit. Think of a class like an architectural blueprint for a house: it specifies the layout, number of rooms, and features, but it is not a house itself. You use that blueprint to build actual houses — those houses are the objects.

terms.definition: A blueprint or template that defines the structure and behavior of objects.
A concrete realization of a class, created at runtime using the new keyword.
A variable declared directly in a class, typically used to store internal state.
A class member that provides a flexible mechanism to read, write, or compute the value of a private field.
A function defined inside a class that describes a behavior the object can perform.
A special method that runs when an object is created, used to initialize its state.

data.caption: Relationship between a class blueprint and its objects

data.text: In C#, you define a class using the `class` keyword. By convention, class names use PascalCase. The class body is enclosed in curly braces `{}` and can contain fields, properties, constructors, and methods. The `public` access modifier makes the class visible to other code; omitting it defaults to `internal`, restricting access to the same assembly.

data.title: Defining a Simple Class
data.content: A Person class with properties, a constructor, and a method.

data.title: The new Keyword
data.text: The new keyword allocates memory for the object and calls its constructor. Each call to new Person(...) creates a completely independent object with its own copy of the data.

Fields are raw variables that store data inside a class. Properties are the public-facing interface to that data, allowing you to add validation, trigger side effects, or compute values on the fly. The C# convention is to make fields `private` and expose them through `public` properties.

data.title: Fields and Properties
data.content: Comparing raw fields with properties, including validation and computed values.

data.text: Constructors are special methods that run automatically when you create a new object. They have the same name as the class and no return type — not even `void`. C# supports parameterless constructors, parameterized constructors, and the `this()` keyword for constructor chaining. If you don't declare any constructor, the compiler provides a free parameterless one.

data.title: Constructor Chaining
data.content: Using this() to chain constructors and avoid duplicate initialization logic.

data.text: Methods define what objects can do. They can accept parameters, return values, and be marked `virtual` to allow overriding in derived classes. Expression-bodied members (`=>`) are a shorthand for single-expression methods or properties introduced in C# 6+.

data.title: Methods on a Class
data.content: Different method signatures including value returns, void methods, and expression-bodied members.

data.text: For data-centric classes where equality is based on value rather than identity, C# 9 introduced `record` types. Records are immutable by default, provide value-based equality, and have a concise syntax ideal for DTOs (Data Transfer Objects).

data.title: Records vs Classes
data.content: Using record types for immutable data with built-in equality and ToString().

data.title: Exercise: Build a Library Book Class
data.description: Create a Book class that models a book in a library. Include ISBN, Title, Author, and Available status. Add a constructor, a Borrow() method, a Return() method, and an IsAvailable property.
steps: Declare a public class Book with private fields for ISBN, Title, Author, and Available.
Create public properties for ISBN, Title, and Author (auto-implemented).
Create a public bool Available property with a private setter.
Write a constructor that takes ISBN, Title, and Author, and sets Available to true.
Add a public void Borrow() method that sets Available to false.
Add a public void Return() method that sets Available to true.
Override ToString() to return a formatted description of the book.
data.expectedOutcome: You can create Book instances and call Borrow()/Return() to manage availability.

I understand the difference between a field and a property.
items.hint: Fields store data; properties expose it with logic.

items.text: I can write a constructor to initialize an object's state.
items.hint: Constructor name must match the class name exactly.

items.text: I can create objects using the new keyword.
I know when to use a record instead of a class.
items.hint: Use records for immutable, value-based data.

items.question: What is the difference between a class and a struct?
items.answer: Classes are reference types stored on the heap, support inheritance, and allow null. Structs are value types stored on the stack, cannot inherit from other classes, and are copied by value. Use structs for small, lightweight data like coordinates or colors.

items.question: Can a class have multiple constructors?
items.answer: Yes. You can overload constructors with different parameter signatures. Use constructor chaining (this(...)) to share initialization logic and avoid duplication.

items.question: What does the get and set accessor do in a property?
items.answer: get returns the property's value; set assigns a new value via the implicit value parameter. You can add validation in set, make one accessor private, or omit one entirely for read-only or write-only properties.

items.question: What is an auto-implemented property?
items.answer: A shorthand syntax like public string Name { get; set; } where the compiler automatically creates a hidden backing field. Use these when you don't need custom validation or logic in the get/set accessors.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Classes bundle data (fields/properties) and behavior (methods) together.
Objects are runtime instances of a class, created with the new keyword.
Properties provide controlled access to private fields with optional validation.
Constructors initialize a new object's state when it is created.
Records (C# 9+) offer concise immutable types with value-based equality.
data.takeaway: Classes and objects form the core building blocks of every C# application.
